question: Who is really falling?

scene.title: Who is really falling?
scene.subtitle: One toss, seen from the ground and from the ball’s perspective. A bathroom scale decides which view tells the truth.
scene.takeaway: Falling needs no push; staying put does. A scale on the falling ball reads zero, while yours reads your weight.

beats.title: What straight means
beats.body: Far from any planet or star, a ball you let go of moves at a steady speed: a straight line on the chart. Nothing pushes it or you: a scale on either would read zero.

beats.title: From the ground
beats.body: On the ground, the toss comes back in an arc. We say gravity pulls the ball, yet a scale riding on it reads zero. You feel the same weightlessness in mid-jump. Scales measure pushes, and only yours reads anything: the ground pushing up on you.

beats.title: From the ball’s perspective
beats.body: Watch the same toss from the ball’s perspective. Its line is straight, as it was far from any planet. Floating doesn’t need you to be far from planets, only that nothing pushes you. At first the ground drops away, since you threw the ball up. Then the Earth below pushes the ground back up to the ball.

beats.title: Which view is right?
beats.body: Both views show the same toss, so a measurement must decide. A scale riding on the ball reads zero, while yours reads your weight. So the ball is the one nothing pushes, and you are the one being pushed. Nothing needs to pull the ball: what needs a cause is you staying put.

scene.why: It turns the usual picture around: falling needs no force, and what you feel as your weight is the ground pushing you.
scene.opening: You toss a ball and catch it. Which is really being pushed: the ball, or you?

questions.q: A scale riding on the tossed ball reads zero the whole time. What does that tell you?
questions.a: Nothing pushes the ball while it flies, so its path is the one that needs no cause.

questions.q: Seen from the ball, which way does the ground move during the toss?
questions.a: Away at first, because of the toss, then back up to the ball, pushed by the Earth beneath it.

questions.q: Why does your scale read your weight while you stand still?
questions.a: The ground pushes up on you through the scale, and that push is what the scale measures.
